name: EGCG-glucoside

lead: EGCG-glucoside is a sugar-linked version of EGCG, the main catechin in green tea. It is named as one of the two components of Redensyl, a cosmetic active used on thinning scalp hair, alongside DHQG.

The appeal is thicker-looking hair through increased follicle activity. The only study found on the glucoside itself looked at a digestive enzyme in a lab dish, not hair; EGCG has wider research in other areas.

paras: It is used as part of Redensyl-type leave-on scalp serums, applied regularly over months and often alongside other thinning-hair products.
High oral intakes of EGCG are linked to liver toxicity according to EFSA. No safety data for the topical glucoside were found.

angle.text: EGCG-glucoside is the green-tea-derived partner of DHQG in Redensyl, a cosmetic active for thinning hair. People use it hoping for more follicle activity and thicker-looking hair. Hair data on this component alone are lacking.

lead: EGCG-glucoside (also called EGCG2 or EGCG-G1) is a glucosylated form of epigallocatechin gallate (EGCG), the main catechin in green tea. In hair-care products it is one of the two named actives in Redensyl, an ingredient from the Induchem biotechnology company, alongside dihydroquercetin-glucoside (DHQG) derived from larch [1]. Redensyl is added to scalp serums aimed at people who want thicker-looking hair and a fuller hairline, and it is also discussed for beard and brow products.

A 2014 trade-press feature on Redensyl, based on the developer's materials, describes the ingredient as combined with glycine and zinc and says it activates hair-follicle bulge stem cells, pushes them toward the growth (anagen) phase, supports dermal papilla cells and reduces scalp inflammation. EGCG2 is the component linked in those materials to the anti-inflammatory role [1]. The same article reports company-run tests in which Redensyl scored almost twice as high as minoxidil in an ex vivo assay, and a placebo-controlled trial in volunteers with Norwood grade 3 to 4 alopecia that reported up to 17% more hair over 84 days. The article does not give sample sizes or independent verification [1].

Independent published work on EGCG-glucoside itself is biochemical. A 2012 laboratory study found that EGCG and EGCG-G1 both inhibited the human intestinal enzyme maltase, with IC50 values of about 20 and 31.5 micromolar [2]. A multi-ingredient Redensyl serum has been tested in a cosmetic clinical evaluation, so effects cannot be assigned to this component alone.
infobox: Component of Redensyl, a cosmetic hair ingredient [1]

paras: EGCG-glucoside appears in cosmetic hair-growth serums as part of Redensyl, together with DHQG, glycine and zinc [1]. In the developer's description, DHQG acts on outer root sheath stem cells and EGCG2 on inflammation [1].

A 2014 feature in Cosmetics Business, drawn from Induchem's materials, reports that Redensyl activates bulge stem cells and pushes them toward anagen, protects them from cell death, boosts dermal papilla fibroblast metabolism and reduces scalp inflammation. It reports up to 17% more hair, 9% more anagen hair and 17% fewer falling hairs over 84 days in a double-blind placebo-controlled trial, with 85% of volunteers showing visible growth [1]. These figures are the developer's and the article does not include the underlying data.

EGCG is the most abundant catechin in tea and is poorly absorbed orally. Excessive oral intake has been linked to liver toxicity, the European Food Safety Authority stated in 2018 that intakes of 800 mg or more daily could raise liver risk, and the FDA has issued warning letters to supplement makers over disease claims [3]. These points concern oral EGCG, not topical cosmetic use.

No studies found for EGCG-glucoside alone on hair or any human outcome. A 2012 in vitro study showed that EGCG and EGCG-G1 inhibit human intestinal maltase, an enzyme studied in relation to type 2 diabetes [2]. A multi-ingredient Redensyl serum has been evaluated in a cosmetic study in healthy women.

timeline.event: Cosmetics Business publishes a feature describing Redensyl, which contains EGCG2 and DHQG. [1]
